title: Tracking Neuronal Motility in Live Murine Retinal Explants
author: Aghaizu, Warre-Cornish, et al.

This step describes the retrieval of retinae either from living mice or from retinal explant cultures at desired developmental stage to set them up for live imaging. Herein contained are details on retinal dissection, tissue mounting, and live imaging culture set up. Live imaging experiments were performed on an upright confocal microscope; for an inverted microscope the setup would have to be modified accordingly.1.Retrieval of retina.When isolating retinae from live mice or retinal explant cultures, follow steps ‘a.’ or ‘b.’, respectively.a.Retrieval from live mice.i.Sacrifice mice by cervical dislocation.ii.Enucleate eyes and transfer to ice-cold RPMI 1640 medium using forceps (Figure 1A).iii.Isolate neural retina (tissue composed of cells of the outer nuclear layer, inner nuclear layer, and ganglion cell layer) by dissection under a dissection microscope in ice-cold RPMI 1640 medium by removing all non-neural tissues (cornea, sclera, iris, choroid, lens, optic nerve, retinal pigment epithelium, and ciliary body) using forceps (Figures 1B and 1C).CRITICAL: Upon removal of the lens during retinal dissection, ensure that vitreous is removed as well. Failure to remove vitreous can impede the flattening process (also applies to 1.b.ii).CRITICAL: Care must be taken to remove all pigmented non-neural retinal tissues (retinal pigment epithelium and ciliary body) as the melanin pigment contained in these tissues absorbs the 2-photon infrared light leading to rapid heat-induced tissue damage when the microscope is operated in 2-photon mode (also applied to 1.b.ii).b.Retrieval from retinal explant cultures.i.Transfer retina from explant culture to ice-cold RPMI 1640 medium.ii.Isolate neural retina by dissection under a dissection microscope in ice-cold RPMI 1640 medium by removing lens with forceps.2.Flattening and mounting retina.a.Apply four equidistant radial cuts using fine scissors going halfway towards the centre of the retina. This results in ‘petal’ like retinal segments (Figure 1D).b.Transfer retina in a small drop of RPMI 1640 medium onto the edge portion of a microscopy glass slide using a sterile plastic Pasteur pipette with manually widened opening (Figure 1I) such that photoreceptors face the glass slide and retinal ganglion cells face the user (Figure 1D).c.Carefully flatten retina onto glass slide by unfolding petals using fine forceps. Petals will resist flattening due to natural curvature of the retina. Flattening is aided by removing some of the RPMI 1640 (Figure 1E).CRITICAL: Care must be taken to not introduce tissue damage during flattening and unfolding petals. This may be aided by using a clean, fine brush. Even small tissue disruption may result in visible loss of retinal integrity during live imaging.CRITICAL: (2.c.-3.b.) During these steps, the retina will be exposed to minimal amounts of RPMI 1640 medium at times. Care must be taken to not let the retina dry out.d.After successful flattening, remove most of RPMI 1640 medium using lint-free tissue paper.e.Immediately place a 0.45 μm MF-Millipore™ nitrocellulose membrane on the retina (with ganglion cell layer touching the membrane) making sure tissue is securely mounted on the membrane (Figure 1F).f.Gently transfer membrane-mounted retina back into RPMI 1640 medium by dipping the edge of the glass slide into medium (Figure 1G). The membrane will gradually become visibly hydrated when contacted by the solution, upon completion of which the membrane can be fully transferred using the dissection tools (Figure 1H).3.Setting up imaging dish for live imaging (Figure 2)a.Fix membrane with retina facing up to the bottom of a Ø5.5 cm tissue culture petri dish on a thin layer of vacuum grease.b.To ensure secure mounting and to prevent tissue drifting during live imaging, carefully press down membrane onto vacuum grease using blunt tools. Place a platinum ring over the membrane, the added weight of which should further prevent tissue drifting.c.Fill the dish with 10 mL DMEMgfp-2 live imaging medium.Figure 2Live imaging setup schematic

steps.title: Breed fluorescent reporter mice
steps.instruction: Set up timed‑matings 2.5–4.5 weeks before the intended imaging stage (typically embryonic day E16.5 to post‑natal day P10.5). For rod labeling, mate Nrl.GFP+/+ mice (homozygous breeding). For cone labeling, mate Chrnb4.EGFP mice (hemizygous). For Cre‑expressing rods, mate Nrl.Cre+/− mice (hemizygous). Check for vaginal plugs the morning after a 14–16 h overnight pairing; the plug marks embryonic day E0.5. Gestation lasts 19–21 days (strain dependent). Harvest retinas at the desired developmental stage for live imaging.

steps.title: Electroporate retinae and establish cultures
steps.instruction: Dissect P0.5–1.5 mouse eyes in ice‑cold dissection medium, removing cornea, sclera, iris, choroid, optic nerve, retinal pigment epithelium and ciliary body while leaving the lens in place. Sterilize #5 Dumont forceps and Vannas scissors with 70 % ethanol and work in a sterile tissue‑culture hood. Transfer each retina with a widened plastic Pasteur pipette into an electroporation cuvette containing 1 µg/µL plasmid DNA in PBS (e.g., shDync1h1/EGFP). Incubate 5 min at room temperature (18–21 °C). Align the retina so the apical surface contacts the anode. Deliver 5 × 30 V square pulses, each 50 ms long with 950 ms intervals, avoiding direct electrode contact with the tissue. Allow recovery in pre‑equilibrated (37 °C/5 % CO₂) dissection medium for 5 min, then transfer to pre‑equilibrated culture medium for another 5 min. Place up to three retinae (lens side down) onto a Whatman® Nuclepore™ Track‑Etched membrane floating on 2 mL culture medium in a 6‑well plate; incubate at 37 °C/5 % CO₂ in a sitting drop (one retina per drop). Add 25 µL fresh culture medium to each drop every other day until imaging. Fluorescent expression is typically visible after 1–2 days and fully established by day 3 post‑electroporation.

substeps.instruction: Dissect retinae in ice‑cold medium, remove non‑neural tissues, keep lens.
Sterilize tools with 70 % ethanol; work in sterile hood.
Transfer retinae to cuvette with 1 µg/µL plasmid DNA in PBS; incubate 5 min at 18–21 °C.
Orient retinae with apical side toward anode; electroporate 5 × 30 V, 50 ms pulses, 950 ms intervals.
Recover 5 min in pre‑equilibrated dissection medium (37 °C/5 % CO₂).
Transfer 5 min to pre‑equilibrated culture medium (37 °C/5 % CO₂).
Place up to 3 retinae lens‑side down on membrane floating on 2 mL medium in 6‑well plate; culture at 37 °C/5 % CO₂.
Add 25 µL culture medium to each sitting drop every other day.

steps.title: Retrieve and flatten retina for imaging
steps.instruction: For live‑mouse retrieval, sacrifice the mouse by cervical dislocation, enucleate eyes, and place them in ice‑cold RPMI 1640. Dissect the neural retina under a microscope, removing all non‑neural tissues (including lens, vitreous, pigment epithelium, ciliary body) in ice‑cold RPMI 1640. For explant‑culture retrieval, transfer the cultured retina to ice‑cold RPMI 1640 and remove the lens. Make four equidistant radial cuts halfway to the centre to create ‘petal’ segments. Using a widened plastic Pasteur pipette, place the retina on the edge of a glass slide with photoreceptors facing the glass and ganglion cells facing up. Flatten by unfolding petals with fine forceps, gently removing excess RPMI 1640 as needed. Remove most of the medium with lint‑free tissue, then lay a 0.45 µm MF‑Millipore™ nitrocellulose membrane on the ganglion‑cell side, ensuring secure contact. Dip the slide edge into RPMI 1640 to hydrate the membrane, then fully transfer the membrane‑mounted retina into the medium with dissection tools.

substeps.instruction: Sacrifice mouse (cervical dislocation) and enucleate eyes; keep in ice‑cold RPMI 1640.
Dissect neural retina, removing cornea, sclera, iris, choroid, lens, optic nerve, RPE, ciliary body; also remove vitreous.
For explant cultures, transfer retina to ice‑cold RPMI 1640 and remove lens.
Make four radial cuts halfway to centre (petal formation).
Transfer retina to glass slide edge with widened Pasteur pipette; orient photoreceptors toward glass.
Flatten by unfolding petals with fine forceps; remove excess RPMI 1640 as needed.
Blot excess medium with lint‑free tissue.
Place 0.45 µm nitrocellulose membrane (ganglion‑cell side down) onto retina.
Dip slide edge into RPMI 1640 to hydrate membrane, then transfer whole assembly into medium.

steps.title: Prepare imaging dish
steps.instruction: Fix the membrane‑mounted retina (ganglion‑cell side down) onto the bottom of a Ø5.5 cm tissue‑culture petri dish using a thin layer of vacuum grease; press gently with blunt tools and place a platinum ring on top to prevent drift. Fill the dish with 10 mL DMEMgfp‑2 live‑imaging medium.

substeps.instruction: Apply thin vacuum‑grease layer to bottom of Ø5.5 cm dish.
Place membrane‑mounted retina (ganglion side down) onto grease; press gently with blunt tool.
Add a platinum ring over the membrane for extra weight.
Add 10 mL DMEMgfp‑2 imaging medium to fill dish.

steps.title: Process tracking data in Matlab
steps.instruction: Export IMARIS‑generated cell‑track files and arrange them in Excel exactly as Table 1 (columns: #, Trajectory ID, Time index, Position x, Position y, Position z). Open and run the Matlab script MSDforztrackingdata.m (available on the project GitHub) and specify the trajectory ID range (e.g., group = [1,2,3];). The script computes average mean‑squared displacement (AvMSD) and standard‑error values for each time lag. Next, run ztrajectory_gen.m to convert the trajectory array into a matrix ‘ztrajectories’, handling leading and trailing NaNs as in the provided code. Then run Trajectory_analysis.m to obtain smoothed instantaneous velocity (dfff2) and acceleration (d2fff2) matrices; the script assumes recordings at 10 min intervals and divides velocity differences by 10 to yield μm/min. Finally, plot AvMSD ± SE versus time lag (0, 10, 20, … min) and fit linear (slope = 2D) or quadratic (y = a x²) models to extract diffusion coefficients or directed‑motion parameters. Also plot histograms of instantaneous velocity and acceleration. All scripts are available at https://github.com/RPearsonLab/Photoreceptor_tracking.

substeps.instruction: Export IMARIS tracking data and format in Excel per Table 1.
Run MSDforztrackingdata.m, set group = [list of trajectory IDs].
Run ztrajectory_gen.m to create ztrajectories matrix (handle NaNs).
Run Trajectory_analysis.m to compute smoothed velocity (dfff2) and acceleration (d2fff2); note 10 min frame interval.
Plot AvMSD ± SE versus time lag; fit linear (2D) or quadratic (a x²) models.
Plot histograms of instantaneous velocity and acceleration.

description: This protocol was designed to track motions of fluorescently labeled retinal cells. In Aghaizu et al. (2021), cellular labeling was achieved either by using transgenic mouse lines expressing cell-type specific fluorescent reporters or by electroporation of acutely explanted retinae with an expression plasmid driving the expression of a fluorescent protein. All mice in preparation of this manuscript were used according to the NC3R ARRIVE guidelines. Both male and female mice were used in this study without discrimination. All animal studies were carried out under the Animals (Scientific Procedures) Act 1986 under a project license PPL 70/8120 issued by the UK Government Home Office and conducted in accordance with protocols approved by the Animal Welfare and Ethics Committee of the UCL Institute of Ophthalmology. All animals were killed by cervical dislocation performed by trained personnel (approved under Schedule 1 as a method of humane killing). All efforts were made to minimize the number and suffering of animals used in these experiments. Male and female mice were group housed in the animal facility at University College London on a standard 12-h light/dark cycle at the same light levels throughout the experimental period. Animals were kept in individually ventilated cages on animal grade wood chips and given access to nesting material and food and water ad libitum.
